newsitem.title: UK: Clinton says Bosnia peace behind schedule.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says Bosnia peace behind schedule.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Thursday the Bosnian peace process was behind schedule and great efforts were needed to stabilise the country if U.S. troops were to leave on time in June 1998.

"I think we would all admit that a lot of the elements of the Bosnia peace process, the Dayton process, are not going as fast as they should," Clinton told a news conference with British Prime Minister Tony Blair. "We are behind schedule."
"If we work like crazy in the next 13 months, do I believe we can fulfil our mission?...Yes I do," he added. "But I think we're going to have to make some very tough decisions."
The United States has about 8,500 peacekeeping troops in Bosnia as part of the 31,000 NATO-led stabilisation force (SFOR) which is due to leave the country by June 1998.

The U.S.-brokered 1995 Dayton accords ended the Bosnia war but their so-called civilian aspects, such as resettlement of refugees to rebuild an integrated society, have met with great resistance within the country.
Clinton said he and Blair discussed a variety of ways to speed up the process, including police training in Bosnia.

Some European leaders have openly argued that the troops will have to stay beyond the deadline. One U.S. official suggested the same thing last week, although the State Department spokesman quickly repudiated his statements.
A U.S. official sought to dispell any inference that Clinton's comments suggested that U.S. troops might remain beyond the deadline, although he did not explicitly rule it out.

"We have a mandate for SFOR which ends in June 1998," U.S. deputy national security adviser Jim Steinberg told reporters. "It is the intention and plan that they come out. That is the basis on which we are operating."
Clinton himself did not mince his words in describing the challenge of restoring peace to Bosnia.
"We can't play around with this," he said. "We can't just sort of hang around and then disappear in a year and expect the Dayton process to go forward. We have a lot of work to do in the next year."
He added: "I don't think we ought to be talking about how we're going to leave; I think we ought to be talking about what we're going to do tomorrow and next week and next month."
